title: A parcel service that never loses an order
summary: EnvíaYa delivers 80,000 parcels a day in the Bajío region. Each new order reaches billing, the customer SMS and driver assignment, and a failure in one does not stop the others.

requirements.1: {{s1}} makes the same order-created event reach several independent consumers, without the API knowing how many there are.
requirements.2: {{s2}} receives its copy of each order and keeps it until a worker confirms it was processed; if the worker dies halfway, the order shows up again.
requirements.3: {{s3}} runs the code that assigns a driver only when there are messages, scales on its own and costs nothing in the early morning.
requirements.4: {{s4}} sets aside only the order that fails 5 times so it can be reviewed later, without blocking the line.
requirements.5: {{s5}} receives the drivers' GPS, keeps it for 7 days in order, and analytics reads it again from the beginning as many times as it wants.

s1.explanation: With a Service Bus topic, each subscription receives a copy of the published message, in a one-to-many publish and subscribe pattern. In a queue, by contrast, only one consumer processes each message.

s2.explanation: Autoforwarding is enabled on the topic subscription (the source) and moves its copy into this queue on its own, because Service Bus does not allow receivers on a source with autoforwarding. In peek-lock, if the lock expires without completion, the message becomes available again.
s2.hint_cue: if the worker dies halfway, the order shows up again

s3.explanation: The Service Bus trigger runs the function when messages reach the queue. In Mexico Central, the Flex Consumption plan scales with the pending messages and down to zero; the Linux Consumption plan is closing down there. It completes the message if the function succeeds and abandons it if it fails.

s4.explanation: Each queue has its own dead-letter subqueue. When a message goes over the maximum delivery count (10 by default, configurable), Service Bus moves it there and it stays until someone reviews it. A Blob container does not count deliveries.

s5.explanation: Event Hubs keeps events in ordered partitions for up to 7 days on the Standard tier, and each consumer group picks its offset, even the beginning, to read them again. Stream Analytics processes in memory and does not store its input.
s5.hint_cue: reads it again from the beginning

azure-managed-redis.s2: Azure Managed Redis is an in-memory cache: its lists do not guarantee delivery or bring the order back if the worker dies halfway.

azure-vm.s3: A VM bills while it is running, even with no orders in the early morning, and it does not run on its own for each message in the queue.

azure-blob-storage.s4: A Blob container stores files, but it does not count a message's deliveries or set it aside on its own.
azure-blob-storage.s5: Blob Storage stores files; it has no partitions with offsets for analytics to read the GPS again in order from the beginning.

azure-stream-analytics.s5: Stream Analytics processes the stream in memory and does not store its input data, so analytics cannot read the GPS again.
